description: The datetime, duration and calendarDuration types that represent points in time, elapsed time and calendar-aware time spans, the functions that create, convert, shift and compare them, the legacy serial date number interface, and the stopwatch and CPU timing functions.

tools.name: datetime
tools.description: Creates datetime arrays representing points in time with nanosecond resolution, optional time zone, and a controllable display format. It parses text automatically for common layouts and accepts an explicit InputFormat for anything unusual. Datetime arrays support arithmetic, comparison, sorting and plotting, and are the recommended replacement for serial date numbers and date strings.
tools.usage:
t = datetime
t = datetime(Y, M, D)
t = datetime(Y, M, D, H, MI, S)
t = datetime(DateStrings, 'InputFormat', fmt)
t = datetime(___, 'TimeZone', tz, 'Format', fmt)

parameters.name: Y, M, D, H, MI, S
parameters.description: Year, month, day, hour, minute and second components.

parameters.name: 'InputFormat'
parameters.description: Format of the text being parsed, for example 'dd/MM/yyyy HH:mm'.

parameters.name: 'Format'
parameters.description: Display format of the resulting datetime.

tools.example:
t = datetime(2025, 3, 14, 15, 9, 26)
t.Format = 'yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm:ss';
t2 = datetime('14/03/2025', 'InputFormat', 'dd/MM/yyyy')
tz = datetime('now', 'TimeZone', 'UTC')
t + days(10)
tools.notes: Datetime format characters follow the Unicode CLDR convention, so MM is month and mm is minute; getting these backwards is the most common mistake. Comparing datetimes with and without a time zone raises an error.

tools.name: duration
tools.description: Creates duration arrays representing fixed lengths of time in hours, minutes and seconds, independent of any calendar. Durations arise naturally from subtracting two datetimes and can be added back to a datetime. Use them for elapsed times, timeouts and sample intervals.
tools.usage:
d = duration(H, MI, S)
d = duration(H, MI, S, MS)
d = duration(X)
d = duration(___, 'Format', fmt)
tools.example:
d = duration(1, 30, 0)
d.Format = 'hh:mm:ss';
elapsed = datetime(2025,3,14,18,0,0) - datetime(2025,3,14,15,9,26)
hours(elapsed)
duration(0, 0, 90)
tools.notes: Durations are exact spans of time and know nothing about months or daylight saving; use `calendarDuration` when adding a month or a calendar day must respect the calendar. Setting Format to 'h' displays the total as a decimal number of hours.

tools.name: calendarDuration
tools.description: Creates calendar-aware time spans in years, months, days and time, where the actual elapsed time depends on when the span is applied. Adding one calendar month to 31 January gives 28 February, and adding a calendar day across a daylight saving transition may be 23 or 25 hours. Use it whenever the calendar matters rather than a fixed number of seconds.
tools.usage:
L = calendarDuration(Y, M, D)
L = calendarDuration(Y, M, D, H, MI, S)
L = calendarDuration(___, 'Format', fmt)

parameters.name: 'Format'
parameters.description: Which components to display, for example 'ymd' or 'ymdt'.

tools.example:
L = calendarDuration(0, 1, 0)
datetime(2025,1,31) + L
datetime(2025,1,31) + days(31)
calmonths(3) + caldays(10)
tools.notes: Calendar durations cannot be converted to an exact number of seconds without a reference date, which is why `seconds(calmonths(1))` is an error. Use `between` to compute a calendar duration between two datetimes.

tools.name: NaT
tools.description: Creates Not-a-Time values, the datetime equivalent of NaN, used to represent missing or invalid points in time. Use it to preallocate datetime arrays and to mark records with no valid timestamp. Any arithmetic involving NaT produces NaT, and comparisons with NaT are false.
tools.usage:
t = NaT
t = NaT(n)
t = NaT(sz1, ..., szN)
t = NaT(___, 'TimeZone', tz, 'Format', fmt)

parameters.name: sz1,...,szN
parameters.description: Size of the datetime array to create.

parameters.name: 'TimeZone'
parameters.description: Time zone of the resulting array.

tools.notes: Use `isnat` or `ismissing` to detect NaT; equality comparison always returns false, exactly as with NaN. Parsing text that does not match the expected format yields NaT rather than an error when you supply an InputFormat.

tools.name: seconds
tools.description: Converts a number to a duration of that many seconds, or converts a duration to the equivalent number of seconds as a double. The dual behaviour depends on the input type, which makes it convenient for moving between numeric and duration representations. It is the finest-grained member of the fixed-length duration family.

parameters.name: x
parameters.description: Numeric value to convert to a duration.

parameters.name: d
parameters.description: Duration to convert to a number of seconds.

tools.notes: `milliseconds` provides the same round trip at a finer scale. Applying seconds to a calendarDuration is an error because a calendar month has no fixed length.

tools.name: minutes
tools.description: Converts a number to a duration of that many minutes, or a duration to a number of minutes. Use it for timeouts, scheduling offsets and reporting elapsed time in convenient units. It is exact, always treating a minute as 60 seconds.

parameters.name: x
parameters.description: Numeric value to convert to a duration.

tools.example:
minutes(90)
minutes(hours(1.5))
deadline = datetime('now') + minutes(15);
minutes(datetime(2025,1,1,12,0,0) - datetime(2025,1,1,11,0,0))
tools.notes: The result of converting a duration is a double, so it can be plotted and compared numerically. Round-tripping through minutes loses sub-minute precision only if you round the number yourself.

tools.name: hours
tools.description: Converts a number to a duration of that many hours, or a duration to a number of hours. Use it to express elapsed times in a readable unit and to construct offsets such as hours(24). Note that hours(24) is exactly 24 hours, which is not the same as one calendar day across a daylight saving change.

parameters.name: x
parameters.description: Numeric value to convert to a duration.

tools.example:
hours(2.5)
hours(minutes(150))
t0 = datetime(2025,3,29,12,0,0,'TimeZone','Europe/Berlin');
[t0 + hours(24), t0 + caldays(1)]
tools.notes: Across a DST transition, hours(24) and caldays(1) give different wall-clock results, which is exactly the distinction the two types exist to capture.

tools.name: days
tools.description: Converts a number to a fixed-length duration of exactly 24-hour days, or converts a duration to that number of days. Use it for durations measured in days where no calendar effects apply, such as scientific sample spacing. For calendar-aware day arithmetic use `caldays` instead.

parameters.name: x
parameters.description: Numeric value to convert to a duration.

tools.example:
days(1.5)
days(hours(36))
datetime(2025,1,1) + days(30)
datetime(2025,1,1) + calmonths(1)
tools.notes: days(30) and calmonths(1) generally land on different dates. Assigning a duration format of 'd' displays a duration as a decimal number of days.

tools.name: years
tools.description: Converts a number to a fixed-length duration of 365.2425 days per year, the mean Gregorian year, or converts a duration to that number of years. It is intended for approximate scientific use, not for calendar arithmetic. Use `calyears` when you mean an actual calendar year.

parameters.name: x
parameters.description: Numeric value to convert to a duration.

tools.example:
years(1)
days(years(1))
datetime(2024,2,29) + calyears(1)
datetime(2024,2,29) + years(1)
tools.notes: Because a fixed year is 365.2425 days, adding years(1) to a date rarely lands on the same calendar date. Adding calyears(1) to 29 February gives 28 February of the next year.

tools.name: caldays
tools.description: Creates a calendar duration of whole days, which respects daylight saving transitions when added to a zoned datetime. Use it whenever 'the next day' means the same wall-clock time tomorrow rather than exactly 24 hours later. The inverse conversion extracts the number of calendar days from a calendarDuration.

parameters.name: L
parameters.description: calendarDuration from which to extract whole days.

tools.example:
caldays(7)
datetime(2025,3,29,12,0,0,'TimeZone','Europe/Berlin') + caldays(1)
caldays(calmonths(1) + caldays(5))
datetime(2025,1,1) + caldays(0:4)
tools.notes: caldays requires whole numbers; fractional days must be expressed with `days` or a time component. Adding caldays across a DST boundary keeps the local time of day constant.

tools.name: calmonths
tools.description: Creates a calendar duration of whole months, whose length in days depends on which months it spans. Adding it to a datetime keeps the day of the month where possible and clips to the last day otherwise. Use it for monthly schedules, billing periods and financial series.

parameters.name: L
parameters.description: calendarDuration from which to extract whole months.

tools.example:
calmonths(3)
datetime(2025,1,31) + calmonths(1)
datetime(2025,1,15) + calmonths(0:3)
calmonths(calyears(1))
tools.notes: Month arithmetic is not reversible: 31 January plus one month minus one month is 28 February, not 31 January. calmonths(calyears(1)) returns 12.

tools.name: calyears
tools.description: Creates a calendar duration of whole years, keeping the same month and day where possible. Use it for anniversaries, annual reporting periods and age calculations. Adding a calendar year to 29 February yields 28 February in a non-leap year.

parameters.name: L
parameters.description: calendarDuration from which to extract whole years.

tools.example:
calyears(2)
datetime(2024,2,29) + calyears(1)
birth = datetime(1990, 6, 15);
age = floor(calyears(between(birth, datetime('today'), 'years')))
tools.notes: calyears(1) equals calmonths(12) for arithmetic purposes. Age calculation is one of the few places where you genuinely need calendar arithmetic rather than fixed durations.

tools.name: between
tools.description: Computes the calendar duration between two datetimes, broken down into the components you request such as years, months and days. Unlike plain subtraction, which gives an exact duration in hours, it answers calendar questions like 'how many whole months apart are these dates'. Use it for ages, tenure and reporting-period calculations.
tools.usage:
dt = between(t1, t2)
dt = between(t1, t2, components)

parameters.name: t1, t2
parameters.description: Datetime arrays; the result is the span from t1 to t2.

tools.notes: Requesting only 'months' gives whole months and discards the remainder. Plain subtraction returns an exact duration in hours, which is a different and often unwanted answer for calendar questions.

tools.name: caldiff
tools.description: Computes successive calendar differences between the elements of a datetime array, the calendar-aware analogue of `diff`. Use it to measure the spacing of monthly or yearly data and to verify that a date sequence is regular in calendar terms. The output is a calendarDuration array with one fewer element.
tools.usage:
dt = caldiff(t)
dt = caldiff(t, components)
dt = caldiff(t, components, dim)

parameters.name: components
parameters.description: Components to report, such as 'months' or {'months','days'}.

tools.example:
t = datetime(2025, 1:4, 1);
caldiff(t)
caldiff(t, 'days')
diff(t)
caldiff(datetime(2025,[1 3 6],15), 'months')
tools.notes: `diff` on datetimes gives exact durations in hours, which vary between months; caldiff reports one month for each step regardless of month length.

tools.name: dateshift
tools.description: Shifts datetimes to the start or end of a calendar unit, or to the nearest or next occurrence of a named day. Use it to snap timestamps to hour, day, month or year boundaries for grouping and binning, and to find month ends and the next Monday. It is the cleanest way to build calendar-aligned time grids.
tools.usage:
t2 = dateshift(t, 'start', unit)
t2 = dateshift(t, 'end', unit)
t2 = dateshift(t, 'dayofweek', dow)
t2 = dateshift(___, rule)

parameters.name: dow
parameters.description: Day of week as a number 1 to 7 or a name such as 'Monday'.

parameters.name: rule
parameters.description: 'previous', 'next', 'nearest' or an integer number of units to shift.

tools.example:
t = datetime(2025, 3, 14, 15, 9, 26);
dateshift(t, 'start', 'month')
dateshift(t, 'end', 'month')
dateshift(t, 'start', 'hour')
dateshift(t, 'dayofweek', 'Monday', 'next')
dateshift(t, 'start', 'day', 0:3)
tools.notes: Passing a vector as the rule generates a whole sequence of shifted dates in one call, which is a compact way to build month-start grids. 'end' of a unit means the start of the next unit minus the smallest representable amount for some units, so check the exact value you get.

tools.name: timeofday
tools.description: Returns the elapsed time since midnight for each datetime, as a duration. Use it to group observations by hour of day, to build daily profiles, and to compare times across different dates. The date part is discarded entirely.
tools.example:
t = datetime(2025, 3, 14, [9 13 17], 30, 0);
timeofday(t)
hours(timeofday(t))
t(timeofday(t) > hours(12))
tools.notes: For zoned datetimes on a daylight saving transition day, the time of day still measures from local midnight, so it can exceed 24 hours in rare cases. Use `hour(t)` when you only need the integer hour.

tools.name: isbetween
tools.description: Tests whether each datetime falls inside a closed interval defined by two endpoints, returning a logical array. Use it to filter observations to a date window, and to validate that timestamps lie within an expected range. Interval inclusivity can be controlled since R2020b.
tools.usage:
tf = isbetween(t, tlower, tupper)
tf = isbetween(t, tlower, tupper, intervalType)

parameters.name: t
parameters.description: Datetime or duration array to test.

tools.notes: For timetables, `timerange` combined with row-time subscripting is more idiomatic than building a logical mask by hand.

tools.name: day
tools.description: Extracts the day component of a datetime, with an option to return the day of month, day of week, day of year or a name. The sibling functions year, quarter, month, week, hour, minute and second extract the other components. Use them for grouping, filtering and building labels.
tools.example:
t = datetime(2025, 3, 14);
day(t)
day(t, 'dayofweek')
day(t, 'name')
[year(t) month(t) hour(t)]
month(t, 'shortname')
tools.notes: Day of week is numbered with Sunday as 1. `week` similarly accepts 'weekofyear' and 'weekofmonth', and `month` accepts 'name' and 'shortname'.

tools.name: week
tools.description: Returns the week number of a datetime, either the week of the year or the week of the month. Use it for weekly aggregation and reporting. Week numbering follows the convention that week 1 contains 1 January.
tools.example:
t = datetime(2025, 1, 1:14);
week(t)'
week(datetime(2025,3,14), 'weekofmonth')
dateshift(t, 'start', 'week')
tools.notes: MATLAB's week numbering is not the ISO 8601 convention, where week 1 is the week containing the first Thursday; compute ISO weeks manually if you need them. Grouping by `dateshift(t,'start','week')` avoids year-boundary ambiguity.

tools.name: weekday
tools.description: Returns the day of the week as a number from 1 (Sunday) to 7 (Saturday), and optionally its name. It accepts datetimes, serial date numbers and date character vectors, which makes it convenient in mixed legacy code. Use it to filter weekends or to build day-of-week aggregates.
tools.usage:
d = weekday(t)
[d, name] = weekday(t)
[d, name] = weekday(t, form)
[d, name] = weekday(t, language)

parameters.name: t
parameters.description: Datetime, serial date number or date text.

tools.example:
[d, nm] = weekday(datetime(2025, 3, 14))
weekday(datetime(2025,3,10:16))'
t = datetime(2025,3,10:16);
t(ismember(weekday(t), [1 7]))
tools.notes: Numbering starts at Sunday, unlike the ISO convention that starts at Monday. For modern code, `day(t,'dayofweek')` and `day(t,'name')` are clearer.

tools.name: datestr
tools.description: Converts datetimes or serial date numbers to formatted character arrays using a numeric or textual format specification. It is the legacy display function that predates the datetime type's own Format property. Use it when interfacing with older code or file formats that expect specific date strings.
tools.usage:
chr = datestr(t)
chr = datestr(t, formatOut)
chr = datestr(DateNumber, formatOut)

parameters.name: t
parameters.description: Datetime array, serial date number or date text.

parameters.name: formatOut
parameters.description: Predefined format number (0 to 31) or a format string such as 'dd-mmm-yyyy HH:MM:SS'.

tools.example:
datestr(datetime(2025,3,14,15,9,26))
datestr(now, 'yyyy-mm-dd HH:MM:SS')
datestr(now, 30)
datestr(738000)
tools.notes: datestr format characters differ from datetime Format characters: here mm is month and MM is minute, the opposite of the datetime convention. New code should set the datetime Format property or use `string(t, fmt)` instead.

tools.name: datenum
tools.description: Converts dates to serial date numbers, the legacy representation counting days since 0 January 0000 with fractional days for the time. Serial date numbers are plain doubles, which is why older code and some file formats still use them. Convert back with `datetime(dn, 'ConvertFrom', 'datenum')`.
tools.usage:
dn = datenum(t)
dn = datenum(Y, M, D)
dn = datenum(Y, M, D, H, MI, S)
dn = datenum(DateString, formatIn)

parameters.name: Y, M, D, H, MI, S

tools.example:
dn = datenum(2025, 3, 14)
datetime(dn, 'ConvertFrom', 'datenum')
datenum('14-Mar-2025')
diff(datenum([2025 1 1; 2025 2 1]))
tools.notes: Serial date numbers lose precision for sub-second times because a double cannot resolve microseconds over a two-thousand-year span. Prefer datetime for all new code; datenum remains only for compatibility.

tools.name: datevec
tools.description: Splits dates into a six-column matrix of year, month, day, hour, minute and second components. Use it when you need numeric components from legacy date representations, or to interface with code that expects date vectors. For datetime arrays the component functions year, month and day are clearer.
tools.usage:
DateVector = datevec(t)
DateVector = datevec(DateString, formatIn)
[Y, M, D, H, MI, S] = datevec(___)

parameters.name: t
parameters.description: Datetime, serial date number or date text.

tools.example:
datevec(datetime(2025,3,14,15,9,26))
[y, m, d] = datevec(now);
[y m d]
datevec('14-Mar-2025 15:09:26')
tools.notes: The seconds column is fractional, so it can carry sub-second information. Two-digit years in text input are interpreted by a pivot year rule, which is a classic source of ambiguity.

tools.name: now
tools.description: Returns the current date and time as a serial date number. It is the legacy counterpart of `datetime('now')` and appears in older timing and logging code. Use datetime in new code, because serial date numbers cannot represent time zones and lose sub-second precision.
tools.example:
t = now
datestr(t)
datetime(t, 'ConvertFrom', 'datenum')
datetime('now')
tools.notes: `now` reflects the system clock in local time with no time zone attached. For elapsed-time measurement use `tic`/`toc` rather than differencing calls to now, which is far less precise.

tools.name: clock
tools.description: Returns the current date and time as a six-element date vector, with a fractional seconds component. It is a legacy function retained for compatibility and for building timestamped file names in older code. `datetime('now')` is the modern replacement.
tools.example:
c = clock
sprintf('%04d%02d%02d_%02d%02d%02.0f', c)
datetime('now')
datestr(clock, 'yyyy-mm-dd')
tools.notes: clock is not monotonic: system clock adjustments can make a later call return an earlier time, so never use it to measure elapsed time. Use `tic`/`toc` for intervals.

tools.name: tic
tools.description: Starts a stopwatch timer for measuring elapsed wall-clock time, optionally returning a timer identifier so that several independent timers can run at once. Use it with `toc` to measure how long a block of code takes. The underlying clock is monotonic and has microsecond resolution.
tools.notes: A bare `tic` overwrites the global timer, so nested timing must use the timerVal form. For reliable benchmarks use `timeit`, which repeats the call and removes measurement overhead.

tools.name: toc
tools.description: Reads the elapsed wall-clock time since the matching `tic`, printing it when called without an output and returning seconds when an output is requested. Pass the identifier from `tic` to read a specific timer. Use it for quick profiling and for progress reporting in long computations.
tools.notes: toc measures wall-clock time, so it includes time spent on other processes; `cputime` measures processor time instead. Timings of very fast operations are dominated by overhead, so use `timeit`.

tools.name: cputime
tools.description: Returns the total CPU time in seconds used by MATLAB since it started. Differencing two calls gives the processor time consumed by the code in between, which excludes time spent waiting. Use it to distinguish computation-bound code from I/O-bound or blocked code.
tools.notes: On multithreaded operations, CPU time can exceed wall-clock time because it sums across cores. `pause` consumes wall-clock time but almost no CPU time, which makes the two measures easy to tell apart.

tools.name: timezones
tools.description: Lists the IANA time zones MATLAB recognizes, as a table with names, UTC offsets and daylight saving offsets, optionally filtered by area or by offset range. Use it to discover valid zone names before setting the TimeZone property of a datetime. The table can be searched with ordinary table filtering.
tools.usage:
T = timezones
T = timezones(area)
T = timezones(lowerOffset, upperOffset)
tools.notes: Changing the TimeZone property of an existing zoned datetime converts the instant to that zone rather than reinterpreting the wall-clock time; assigning a zone to an unzoned datetime does the reinterpretation.

tools.name: posixtime
tools.description: Converts datetimes to POSIX time, the number of seconds since 1970-01-01 00:00:00 UTC, ignoring leap seconds. Use it when exchanging timestamps with databases, web APIs, log formats and other languages. Convert back with `datetime(p, 'ConvertFrom', 'posixtime')`.

parameters.name: t
parameters.description: Datetime array; must have a TimeZone set.

tools.example:
t = datetime(2025, 3, 14, 'TimeZone', 'UTC');
p = posixtime(t)
datetime(p, 'ConvertFrom', 'posixtime', 'TimeZone', 'UTC')
posixtime(datetime('now','TimeZone','local'))
tools.notes: posixtime requires a zoned datetime; an unzoned input raises an error because the instant would be ambiguous. Related converters include `juliandate`, `exceltime` and `yyyymmdd`.
